question_text: What is the difference between 'interface' and 'type' in TypeScript?
correct_answer: Both define object shapes but have key differences. Interfaces support declaration merging (you can add to them in separate files) and are generally preferred for object shapes and class contracts. Type aliases can represent primitives, unions, intersections, tuples, and mapped types — things interfaces cannot do. In practice: use interface for public API definitions and OOP-style contracts, use type for complex type compositions, unions (string | number), and utility types.
key_points: Interface: declaration merging, extendable, preferred for OOP
Type: unions, intersections, primitives, more flexible
Interface cannot represent union types — type can
Prefer interface for object shapes, type for complex compositions
tip: Show a union type example — type Status = 'active' | 'inactive' cannot be written as interface.

question_text: Explain TypeScript generics with a practical example.
correct_answer: Generics allow writing reusable code that works with multiple types while preserving type safety. Instead of using 'any', a generic placeholder (T) is used that gets resolved at call time. Example: function identity<T>(arg: T): T { return arg; } — calling identity<string>('hello') enforces the return type is string. Generics are used in collections, API response wrappers, and utility functions. Constraints like <T extends object> limit what types are accepted.
key_points: T is a type placeholder resolved at call time
Avoids any — preserves type safety across types
Constraints: <T extends SomeType> for narrowing
Generic interfaces and classes work the same way
tip: Show a generic API response wrapper: type ApiResponse<T> = { data: T; error: string | null } — very practical.

question_text: What are TypeScript utility types and name the most commonly used ones?
correct_answer: Utility types are built-in mapped types that transform existing types. Partial<T> makes all properties optional. Required<T> makes all required. Readonly<T> prevents mutation. Pick<T, K> selects specific keys. Omit<T, K> removes specific keys. Record<K, V> creates a map type. ReturnType<T> extracts a function's return type. Exclude<T, U> removes union members. These enable DRY type reuse without duplicating type definitions.
key_points: Partial: all optional, Required: all mandatory
Pick/Omit: create subtypes by selecting or removing keys
Record<string, User>: typed map/dictionary pattern
ReturnType<typeof fn>: extract return type automatically
tip: Show Partial in form handling: function updateUser(id: string, updates: Partial<User>) — real-world pattern.

question_text: What is the difference between 'unknown' and 'any' in TypeScript?
correct_answer: Both represent values whose type is not known at compile time, but they behave differently. 'any' completely disables type checking — you can do anything with it. 'unknown' is the type-safe counterpart — you must narrow the type before using it (typeof, instanceof, or a type guard). Prefer unknown over any for external input (API responses, user input) because it forces you to check before using. any is an escape hatch that should be minimized.
key_points: any: disables type checking entirely — anything goes
unknown: must narrow with typeof/instanceof before use
unknown is the safe version of any for external data
never: opposite of unknown — no values exist for this type
tip: Use unknown for JSON.parse() return type — forces callers to validate the structure before use.

question_text: Explain TypeScript decorators and their use cases.
correct_answer: Decorators are a TypeScript feature (currently at TC39 stage 3) that add metadata or modify behavior of classes, methods, properties, and parameters. Class decorators run with the constructor, method decorators wrap the method, property decorators attach metadata. Used heavily in NestJS (Controller, Injectable, Get), Angular (Component, Injectable), and TypeORM (Entity, Column). They implement the Decorator design pattern. Require experimentalDecorators: true in tsconfig.
key_points: Four types: class, method, property, parameter decorators
Used in NestJS, Angular, TypeORM heavily
Implement Decorator design pattern
Require experimentalDecorators in tsconfig.json
tip: Mention NestJS @Injectable() and @Controller() as real-world decorator usage — shows framework context.

question_text: What is type narrowing in TypeScript and what techniques are used?
correct_answer: Type narrowing reduces a broad type (like string | number) to a specific type using runtime checks. Techniques: typeof guard (typeof x === 'string'), instanceof check (x instanceof Date), in operator (if ('name' in obj)), discriminated unions (checking a literal type field like type: 'circle'), truthiness narrowing (if (x)), and type predicates (function isString(x: any): x is string). TypeScript's control flow analysis understands these and narrows types in branches.
key_points: typeof guard for primitive narrowing
instanceof for class instance narrowing
Discriminated unions: switch on a literal type tag
User-defined type predicates: x is Type syntax
tip: Discriminated union pattern: type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number } | { kind: 'square'; side: number } — show switch narrowing.

question_text: How does TypeScript handle null and undefined? What is strict null checking?
correct_answer: Without strictNullChecks, null and undefined are assignable to any type — a common source of runtime errors. With strictNullChecks: true (part of strict mode), null and undefined are their own distinct types. You must explicitly include them in unions (string | null) and handle them before use. Optional chaining (obj?.prop) safely navigates null. Nullish coalescing (??) provides a default when null/undefined. Non-null assertion (!) tells TypeScript a value is definitely not null.
key_points: strictNullChecks prevents null/undefined assignment to other types
Optional chaining (?.) safe navigation
Nullish coalescing (??) vs OR (||) — only null/undefined vs falsy
Non-null assertion (!) — use sparingly, defeats safety
tip: Difference between ?? and ||: false ?? 'default' = false, but false || 'default' = 'default'.

question_text: What are mapped types in TypeScript and how do you create custom ones?
correct_answer: Mapped types create new types by iterating over keys of an existing type. Syntax: type Mapped<T> = { [K in keyof T]: TransformedType }. The built-in utilities (Partial, Readonly, Required) are all implemented as mapped types. You can add modifiers (+ or -) to add or remove optional/readonly. Conditional types within mapped types enable complex transformations. Example: type Nullable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null }.
key_points: [K in keyof T] iterates over all keys of T
Built-in utilities are mapped types under the hood
-? removes optional, -readonly removes readonly
Combine with conditional types for advanced transformations
tip: Implement Partial yourself: type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] } — shows deep understanding.

question_text: Explain conditional types in TypeScript with an example.
correct_answer: Conditional types follow a ternary syntax: T extends U ? X : Y. If T is assignable to U, the type is X, otherwise Y. Used in utility types: NonNullable<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T. They enable type inference within the condition using 'infer'. Example: type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never — extracts the return type of any function. Distributive conditional types automatically apply to each member of a union.
key_points: T extends U ? X : Y — ternary for types
infer keyword extracts a type within a condition
Distributive: applies to each union member automatically
NonNullable and ReturnType built using conditional types
tip: Show infer in a real example: type UnpackArray<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T — extracts element type.

question_text: How do you configure TypeScript with tsconfig.json? What are the most important options?
correct_answer: tsconfig.json controls TypeScript compilation. Key options: strict (enables all strict checks including strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes), target (ES2015/ES2020 — output JS version), module (commonjs/es2020 — module system), outDir (compiled output folder), include/exclude (files to compile). For modern projects: strict: true is essential. esModuleInterop enables default imports from CommonJS modules. paths enables path aliases. jsx: 'react-jsx' for React projects.
key_points: strict: true is the most important setting
target: output JavaScript version
module: commonjs (Node.js) or es2020 (bundlers)
paths: module path aliases for clean imports
tip: strict: true catches 80% of runtime bugs at compile time — always enable it for new projects.

question_text: What are discriminated unions and when do you use them?
correct_answer: A discriminated union is a union of types that all share a common literal type field (the discriminant). Example: type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number } | { kind: 'rect'; width: number; height: number }. When you switch on the 'kind' field, TypeScript narrows each case perfectly. They're used for state machines, action types (Redux), API response variants, and any scenario with mutually exclusive states. Exhaustive checking with never in the default case.
key_points: Shared literal type field (discriminant) enables narrowing
switch/if on discriminant narrows type in each branch
Used for Redux actions, state machines, API variants
Default: never case catches unhandled union members
tip: Redux action types are classic discriminated unions — type Action = { type: 'INCREMENT' } | { type: 'RESET', to: number }.

question_text: How do you use TypeScript with React? What are the common type patterns?
correct_answer: In React TypeScript: function components typed with React.FC<Props> or just (props: Props) => JSX.Element. Props interface defines component API. State types inferred or explicit: useState<User | null>(null). Event handlers: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>. Children: React.ReactNode (most permissive) or React.ReactElement. Refs: React.useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) with type. Avoid React.FC for simple components — it's verbose and unnecessary.
key_points: Props interface for component type safety
Generic useState<Type> for complex state
React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> for event handlers
React.ReactNode vs ReactElement vs JSX.Element
tip: Use ComponentProps<typeof Comp> to extract and extend existing component prop types.

question_text: What is the 'satisfies' operator in TypeScript (4.9+)?
correct_answer: The 'satisfies' operator validates that an expression matches a type without widening it. Difference from assignment: const palette = { red: [255,0,0] } satisfies Record<string, number[]> — TypeScript knows palette.red is number[] not number[] | string[]. With a regular type annotation, you lose the specific types. 'satisfies' gives you both validation AND type inference preservation. Useful for configuration objects where you want autocompletion of known keys.
key_points: Validates against a type without losing specific type info
Different from annotation: preserves literal and specific types
Great for config objects, route definitions, color palettes
Added in TypeScript 4.9
tip: satisfies is like getting type checking AND inference — the best of both worlds for config objects.

question_text: What are TypeScript enums and what are their alternatives?
correct_answer: TypeScript enums define named constants. Numeric enums auto-increment from 0, string enums require explicit values. They compile to JavaScript objects. Const enums are inlined at compile time (no JS object). Problems: numeric enums allow any number assignment (not type-safe), reverse mappings bloat output, string enums are better. Alternatives: union of literal strings (type Direction = 'North' | 'South'), or as const assertion on object ({ NORTH: 'north' } as const).
key_points: String enums safer than numeric enums
Const enums inlined at compile — no runtime overhead
Union literals: type Status = 'active' | 'inactive' — simpler
as const on object gives enum-like behavior without enum
tip: Most TypeScript teams now prefer as const object or union literals over enums — explain the reasons.

correct_answer: Declaration merging allows multiple declarations of the same name to merge into a single definition. Interface merging: two interface blocks with the same name combine their members. Module augmentation: add properties to existing module types (augmenting Express Request with user property). Namespace merging with functions/classes: add static members to functions. Used heavily for extending third-party library types in @types packages.
key_points: Interface declarations with same name merge their members
Module augmentation extends third-party library types
Commonly used to add req.user to Express Request
Type aliases cannot be merged — only interfaces
tip: Show Express Request augmentation: declare namespace Express { interface Request { user?: User } } — real pattern.
